title: Fairchild’s dollar-bill contract
fact: When Fairchild’s eight founders received their initial funding, bankers Arthur Rock and Bud Coyle handed them eight new dollar bills and suggested they sign them as a contract with one another.
explanation: After eight engineers left Shockley Semiconductor, they spent several months trying to establish a new company devoted to making silicon transistors. Their breakthrough came when they connected with entrepreneur Sherman Fairchild and secured initial funding with help from bankers Arthur Rock and Bud Coyle. The bankers’ memorable gesture—handing each founder a brand-new dollar bill to sign as a contract with the others—captured the trust and partnership behind Fairchild Semiconductor. The signed bills became a small but vivid artifact of the company’s beginning; the copy shown in the Stanford University Libraries collection belonged to founder Jay Last. Fairchild soon became central to Silicon Valley’s semiconductor culture, including Bob Noyce’s 1959 invention of the integrated circuit while working there.

title: Ronald Wayne breaks the tie
fact: On April 1, 1976, Ronald Wayne mediated a dispute between Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, drafted Apple’s partnership agreement, and became its third cofounder with a 10% stake before backing out 12 days later.
explanation: On April 1, 1976, Ronald Wayne helped settle a disagreement between Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak as they were forming what became Apple. Wayne wrote a partnership agreement and joined the two Steves as Apple’s third cofounder, holding 10 percent of the company so he could break ties when they disagreed. His role shows that Apple’s origin was not only a story of engineering and product ideas, but also of early decisions about control, intellectual property, and how a small partnership would operate. Wayne withdrew 12 days later. The episode captures the improvised, personal character of Apple’s beginnings before the company grew from its roots in a garage into a major technology enterprise.

title: Apple’s IPO makes overnight millionaires
fact: When Apple went public in 1980, employees who owned founder’s stock became millionaires overnight.
explanation: Apple’s 1980 initial public offering marked a turning point for Silicon Valley, which was still establishing itself as an enclave of high technology. Employees who owned the company’s founder’s stock became millionaires overnight, demonstrating that working at a technology startup could produce extraordinary personal wealth. The event showed the wider public that technology was “hot,” valuable, and accessible as an investment, helping make the IPO a defining symbol of the Valley. It also brought greater attention to Steve Jobs, whose informal appearance helped establish the image of the “casual rockstar CEO.” Apple’s offering therefore connected employee ownership, entrepreneurial risk, public markets, and a new technology-centered culture of fame and fortune.

title: Wozniak shares the Apple I
fact: Steve Wozniak displayed his Apple I and shared its design details at the Homebrew Computer Club, where few predicted it would seed a major company.
explanation: In the mid-1970s, the Homebrew Computer Club brought designers, hackers, entrepreneurs, and hobbyists together around the San Francisco Bay Area’s emerging personal-computer scene. Members commonly displayed their creations in the SLAC auditorium’s anteroom, explaining what they had built and sharing hardware and software details. Steve Wozniak did this with the Apple I, presenting a design that engineers admired even though few attendees expected it to become the foundation of a major company. The setting captures Homebrew’s open, hands-on culture: people gathered around homemade machines, exchanged technical knowledge, and treated microcomputers as practical tools rather than toys. That habit of sharing helped accelerate the shift from expensive computers for institutions toward personal machines that individuals could own.

title: ARPANET’s first message crashes at “lo”
fact: On October 29, 1969, UCLA programmer Charley Kline tried to log in to Bill Duvall’s computer at SRI, but the system crashed after transmitting “lo,” the first message between hosts on ARPANET.
explanation: On the evening of October 29, 1969, Charley Kline worked at a computer terminal at UCLA while Bill Duvall monitored a computer 350 miles away at the Stanford Research Institute in Northern California. Kline was attempting to log in remotely when the network accepted the letters “l” and “o,” then crashed as he typed “g.” The bug was fixed, and the connection was fully operating before the programmers went home. This small, unfinished word marked the first message between hosts on ARPANET, an experimental network built by the US Advanced Research Projects Agency. Its importance came from the larger idea being tested: linking different kinds of computers so previously isolated timesharing systems could exchange information, helping establish the networking culture that shaped Silicon Valley and the modern Internet.

title: Larry Page’s DIY Street View test
fact: In 2003, Google co-founder Larry Page tested street-level filming with a video camera in his own car, then funded a Stanford project to develop the idea at massive scale.
explanation: In 2003, Google co-founder Larry Page explored whether street-level views could be captured on a much larger scale than earlier experimental movie maps. He began with a practical test: filming from a video camera mounted in his own car. Page then funded a Stanford project to develop the idea, linking a do-it-yourself automotive experiment with the research culture surrounding Silicon Valley universities. The effort helped move interactive views of real places from specialized demonstrations toward a web service that ordinary users could access. Earlier systems such as MIT’s Aspen Movie Map had required custom equipment and laserdiscs; Google’s challenge was to make comparable “surrogate travel” workable across many streets. Page’s test captures a characteristic technology pattern: a simple prototype becoming the starting point for ambitious infrastructure.

title: Steve Jobs overlooks the Alto’s network
fact: When Steve Jobs saw a Xerox Alto demonstration, he recognized the potential of its windows and mouse but later said he had overlooked its networking.
explanation: The Xerox Alto, introduced in 1973 by Xerox PARC in Palo Alto, combined a mouse, windows, visual graphics, removable disk storage, and networking in a small computer. According to restorer Al Kossow, Steve Jobs was immediately drawn to the windows and mouse during an Alto demonstration, but later said he had missed the importance of its networking. That oversight is striking because Alto users could connect machines for electronic mail, chat, and other networked activities by the late 1970s. The episode captures a defining Silicon Valley tension: a visible interface can be easier to understand at first glance than the less obvious infrastructure connecting computers together. It also shows how PARC’s experimental systems offered ideas that later shaped personal computing culture.

title: The groundbreaking computer Xerox never sold
fact: About 1,500 Xerox Alto computers were built and deployed, but the groundbreaking machine was never sold as a product.
explanation: The Xerox Alto emerged from Xerox’s Palo Alto Research Center, founded in 1970 to explore the future of electronic office work. Developed as a research prototype beginning in 1972, it combined a bit-mapped 606-by-808-pixel display, keyboard, mouse, local storage, Ethernet networking, and software such as the Bravo WYSIWYG word processor. About 1,500 Altos were eventually built and deployed inside Xerox, at universities, and at other sites, where researchers could create, store, print, and transmit documents across connected systems. Yet Xerox never offered the Alto itself as a commercial product. Its importance lies in how a laboratory machine demonstrated ideas—including windows, menus, direct manipulation, mouse pointing, raster graphics, and networked personal computing—that later shaped mass-market computers and the broader culture of Silicon Valley.

title: Ethernet begins in a Xerox PARC memo
fact: On May 23, 1973, Bob Metcalfe outlined Ethernet in a memo to his managers at Xerox PARC, before Dave Boggs turned the concept into a working network.
explanation: On May 23, 1973, young researcher Bob Metcalfe described a new networking concept in a memo to his managers at Xerox PARC, the research center where advanced computer technologies were being developed. Radio and hardware expert Dave Boggs then helped turn the idea into a working system. Early Ethernet connected Xerox Alto computers with laser printers and remote servers, making it a local network rather than an isolated collection of machines. Its first versions used shared television-style coaxial cable, a practical but difficult medium that was later replaced by telephone-style wiring. The episode captures Silicon Valley’s research culture: a memo inside a laboratory became infrastructure used in offices, homes, data centers, and cafes, with wireless networking later emerging as an offshoot.

title: A Soviet scientist confides in Stanford’s Doctor
fact: In 1965 at Stanford, Soviet computer scientist Andrei Yershov confided intimate worries about his wife and children to the Doctor program despite knowing it was a machine.
explanation: In 1965, Stanford was one of the world’s major centers of artificial-intelligence research, alongside Carnegie Mellon and MIT. Visiting Soviet computer scientist Andrei Yershov asked to see Doctor, an early interactive program developed by psychiatrist Kenneth Colby to explore whether computers could provide therapeutic conversations. Sitting at a teletype machine, Yershov typed that he was tired from traveling and away from home; after Doctor prompted him to discuss his family, he shared intimate worries about his wife and children. Pamela McCorduck, watching the exchange, saw that a text-based machine could draw out an emotional response even when its user knew it was not human. The episode became a vivid early example of AI’s social power—and of the ethical questions raised when software enters deeply personal territory.

title: ImageNet crowdsources the visual world
fact: Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li and her collaborators built ImageNet by collecting internet images and crowdsourcing their labeling to gig workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
explanation: Beginning in 2006, Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li and her graduate students pursued an ambitious idea: creating an image dataset organized around every noun in the English language. They gathered pictures from the internet and classified them using WordNet, a database describing relationships among words. Because the project was enormous, Li’s collaborators outsourced image labeling to gig workers through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk platform. Completed in 2009, ImageNet was larger than any earlier image dataset by several orders of magnitude. Its scale gave computer-vision researchers a shared testing ground and helped supply the data needed for later advances such as AlexNet, linking web-scale information, human labor, and machine-learning research in a landmark chapter of AI history.

title: Pong’s Copycat Crisis
fact: Atari created Al Alcorn’s home version of Pong to regain market share lost to unauthorized arcade copies, but millions of illegal copies of the home game followed.
explanation: In the early 1970s, Atari’s Pong helped create a gaming revolution after its introduction in neighborhood arcades. Engineer Al Alcorn designed a home version around 1974 so Atari could recover market share that unauthorized arcade copies had taken away. The strategy revealed both the appeal and vulnerability of an emerging video-game industry: a simple electronic game could move from arcade cabinets into living rooms, but its design could also be copied at enormous scale. According to the Computer History Museum, millions of illegal copies of the home version followed. The episode connects Silicon Valley’s culture of rapid experimentation with the practical challenges of building a business around new technology, and it places Atari and Alcorn among the lesser-known people whose work helped make computing accessible to mass audiences.

title: Google designed the TPU as a supercomputer
fact: Google’s TPU program was designed as a supercomputer from the beginning.
explanation: Google’s TPU program reflects a shift from treating an AI chip as an isolated component to designing an entire computing system for large-scale workloads. In a CHM discussion, Google’s Norm Jouppi explained that the TPU benefited from being designed as a supercomputer from the beginning, alongside Google’s long-standing investment in optical and large-scale networking technologies. That context matters because modern AI requires massive matrix computation, high memory bandwidth, and fast interconnects rather than only a powerful processor. The TPU therefore represents Silicon Valley’s systems-oriented culture: hardware, networking, software, power, cooling, and operational expertise must work together. Its design also illustrates why major technology companies can draw on experience deploying computing infrastructure at enormous scale.

title: Real-time search arrives at SRI
fact: In 1963, Charlie Bourne, Doug Engelbart, and programmer Lynn Chaitin tested real-time full-text search from SRI on a remote SAGE computer, including Boolean qualifiers such as "and" and "or."
explanation: In 1963, Stanford Research Institute was a setting for an important shift in information retrieval. Charlie Bourne wrote the specification, Lynn Chaitin programmed it, and Doug Engelbart helped conduct a test that searched the full text of documents on a remote computer. The machine was one of the large computers custom-built for the SAGE nuclear-warning system, accessed through ARPA support from J.C.R. Licklider. Search itself was not new: earlier batch systems using punched cards had already demonstrated features such as natural-language queries and relevance scoring. The breakthrough was real-time interaction—searching in a live exchange with the computer instead of submitting cards and waiting. Boolean qualifiers such as "and" and "or" made the experiment an early model of modern online search.

title: Résumés fly at the Wagon Wheel
fact: During the Fairchild Semiconductor era, National Semiconductor defectors visiting local watering holes such as Walker’s Wagon Wheel were pelted with résumés from former colleagues.
explanation: During the Fairchild Semiconductor era, Walker’s Wagon Wheel and nearby watering holes such as Chez Yvonne and Rickey’s became informal meeting places for engineers and entrepreneurs near Fairchild’s Mountain View headquarters. Silicon Valley historian Michael Malone described how National Semiconductor was taking many of Fairchild’s best employees, and how former colleagues responded whenever those defectors appeared: they pelted them with résumés. The episode captures an early form of the Valley’s intensely social labor market, where ideas, techniques, and job opportunities circulated through face-to-face encounters rather than only through formal recruiting. It also shows why physical gathering places mattered to the region’s technology culture: personal networks and employee movement helped create the spinoffs and cross-pollination that drove Silicon Valley’s growth.

title: Passenger rail arrives on the Peninsula
fact: The San Francisco and San Jose Railroad Company began passenger rail service on the Peninsula in 1863.
explanation: In 1863, the San Francisco and San Jose Railroad Company began carrying passengers along the San Francisco Peninsula, creating an early transportation link between San Francisco, the Peninsula communities, and San Jose. The service belongs to a much longer history than the modern Caltrain name: Caltrain’s current system began in 1992, when the Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board took over train operations. This history shows how rail became part of the region’s basic infrastructure, connecting communities along the corridor and supporting the Peninsula’s later economic development. Today, Caltrain describes its role as providing commuter service through the South Bay to San Jose and Gilroy, making the original 1863 passenger line an important foundation for the transportation network associated with the technology region.

title: Fred Terman builds a technical community
fact: Fred Terman recalled setting out to create a community of technical scholars in Silicon Valley when there “wasn’t much here.”
explanation: Fred Terman, a Stanford alumnus, faculty emeritus, and former provost, described an early Silicon Valley that had not yet become a major global technology center. His aim was to build a community of technical scholars in and around Stanford, linking the university to the region’s emerging culture of research and innovation. The contrast in his recollection is central: the area once seemed small beside the rest of the world, while later the world’s technological activity had gathered there. Stanford’s role in developing breakthrough technologies helped shape that transformation. Terman’s papers are held in the Stanford Libraries’ Silicon Valley Archives, where the “Garages & Gadgets” exhibition presents his story alongside sections on electronics, chips, computing, and digital culture.

title: Ray Dolby builds the electronics behind the first videotape recorder
fact: Early in his career at Bay Area-based Ampex, Ray Dolby invented the electronics behind the first videotape recorder.
explanation: Early in his career, Ray Dolby worked at Bay Area-based Ampex, an industry leader in magnetic recording, where he invented the electronics behind the first videotape recorder. The achievement places him within the region’s formative hardware culture, when engineers were developing systems that could capture and reproduce moving images as well as sound. A photograph described by Stanford shows Dolby standing behind the first Ampex videotape recorder, linking the person to the substantial recording device that helped define this new technology. Dolby later became known for sound innovations, but his Ampex work shows how electrical engineering in the Bay Area connected directly to television, entertainment, and recording. Stanford’s archive preserves this intersection of technical invention and media history as part of Silicon Valley’s broader development.

title: Google’s seed funding from a Sun founder
fact: Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin received seed funding from Sun Microsystems cofounder Andy Bechtolsheim after reaching him through a personal connection.
explanation: In the early stage of Google’s development, Larry Page and Sergey Brin obtained seed funding from Andy Bechtolsheim, one of the founders of Sun Microsystems. Paul Graham presents the episode as an example of how startup financing worked before organized seed accelerators: angel investors supplied early money and sometimes useful advice, but were difficult for unknown founders to reach. Page and Brin had an advantage because they knew someone who could make a personal introduction to Bechtolsheim. The story captures an important Silicon Valley pattern—technical founders moving from research and software development toward a company through relationships inside the region’s technology network. It also shows how uncertain a startup could be before it became famous: Google was still a small, vulnerable venture rather than an inevitable success.
